--- 1.1 | Quality and pertinence of the project’s research and innovation objectives (and the extent to which they are ambitious, and go beyond the state of the art) ---
Introduction, objectives and overview of the overall research programme

Despite rapid advances, the current state of AI in healthcare remains correlation-driven, fragmented and poorly adapted to clinical reality. Most deployed models operate as statistical predictors rather than decision technologies and therefore struggle with external validity, transportability and regulatory acceptance. Systematic reviews confirm that adoption is slowed by fragmented data environments, limited explainability and a lack of prospective clinical evidence. In cardiovascular applications, the literature reveals broad enthusiasm but few implementation case studies and no clear pathways for compliance with emerging AI regulations. This leaves hospitals, regulators and patients with "AI as a promise" rather than a demonstrably safe and auditable intervention tool.

The proposal is timely because emerging regulatory and policy frameworks now require trustworthy, explainable and interoperable AI in high-risk healthcare settings. PROJECT-X directly responds to these policy drivers while contributing to broader digital-health and societal objectives through fair, robust AI tools that are clinically actionable across diverse populations.

PROJECT-X’s overarching ambition is:

1. to replace correlation-centric models with causal objectives and counterfactual evaluation;

2. to treat interoperability and governance as first-class design constraints;

3. to embed human-in-the-loop co-creation and targeted stakeholder training;

4. to execute healthcare-embedded case studies that generate evidence on safety, adoption and value.

Together, these elements define a cohesive research programme addressing key skills and knowledge gaps in healthcare AI.

Specific measurable research and innovation objectives

O1 – Trustworthy causal AI (WP1)

Develop explainable, fair and sensitivity-aware causal AI models that articulate assumptions, quantify uncertainty and provide counterfactual “what-if” and cause- effect reasoning at both patient and policy levels.

Success KPIs

• KPI1.1: ≥1 multimodal AI model integrated with causal modules.

• KPI1.2: ≥10 clinicians test the tool and ≥80% report improved confidence in AI- supported decisions.

• KPI1.3: ≥1 joint report or white paper citing causal evidence generated within the project.

O2 – Interoperability for identifiability (WP2)

Establish multimodal, robust and privacy-preserving data flows and the semantic structures required by target causal graphs.

Implement federated identifiability and transportability checks across sites to ensure that models remain valid, generalisable and clinically deployable under heterogeneous real-world conditions.

Success KPIs

• KPI2.1: successful integration of ≥4 data modalities into a unified semantic schema.

• KPI2.2: ≥1 pilot model per use case integrating ≥3 formalised clinical or physiological rules.

• KPI2.3: ≥1 data exchange protocol between academic and industrial partners.

• KPI2.4: ≥1 published guideline or white paper reviewed by technical, clinical and regulatory stakeholders.

O3 – Awareness and co-creation (WP3)

Deliver role-specific training for clinicians, data stewards and regulators; implement human-in-the-loop AI tools; and co-create interfaces with patients to improve usability, trust and real-world alignment.

Success KPIs

• KPI3.1: clinician and patient usability ratings ≥80%.

• KPI3.2: ≥2 co-design workshops with ≥15 participants.

• KPI3.3: ≥3 AI tools supporting interactive clinician feedback and retraining mechanisms.

O4 – Clinical adaptation and evidence (WP4)

Translate AI-based decision support into healthcare practice by identifying practical barriers to deployment.

Conduct retrospective evaluations across:

• Rare Neurodegenerative Cohorts

• Structural Heart Intervention Cohorts

• Heart Failure Cohorts

• population-level studies

• routine clinical workflows

Success KPIs

• KPI4.1: ≥1 health-economic or cost-effectiveness evaluation.

• KPI4.2: ≥2 policy briefs or white papers.

• KPI4.3: implementation of at least one AI system in an additional clinical environment.

Cross-cutting objective (CO)

Operationalise relevant AI regulations and best-practice guidelines across all objectives by embedding:

• transparency

• risk classification

• robustness

• human oversight

• lifecycle monitoring

throughout model development and deployment.

Success KPIs

• Unified compliance and risk-management framework.

• ≥1 regulatory-readiness toolkit publication.

• Dissemination through at least two international channels.

DC1 – Physiology-aware AI for clinical decision support

Host: Research-intensive European university with expertise in biomedical signal processing and explainable AI (WP1, WP2, WP4)

Objectives

• Formalise clinical and physiological knowledge including heuristics, rules, causal relations and constraints for cardiovascular use cases.

• Develop compact physiology-aware AI architectures that integrate domain knowledge at data, model and decision levels.

• Provide transparent explanations and uncertainty estimates that clinicians can interrogate.

Expected Results

• Knowledge representations and software prototypes for physiology-aware AI across multiple imaging and biosignal modalities.

• Demonstration of improved robustness and generalisability compared with black-box baselines.

• Reusable modules supporting explainability and trustworthy AI across the network.

Key Secondments

• University medical centre specialising in cardiovascular clinical workflows and healthcare data infrastructures.

• Engineering school with expertise in causal AI, medical imaging and multimodal analysis.

• Clinical imaging centre providing advanced cardiovascular imaging datasets.

Contribution to the Network

Provides the physiological and mechanistic foundations supporting trustworthiness, interoperability and clinical adaptation.

DC2 – Causal multimodal integration for cardiovascular risk prediction

Host: Technical university with expertise in medical imaging, multimodal AI and causal modelling (WP1, WP2, WP4)

Objectives

• Identify causal estimands across time series, laboratory measurements and biomarkers.

• Develop architectures supporting temporal causal reasoning and counterfactual inference.

• Design multimodal fusion approaches that improve interpretability and robustness.

Expected Results

• Causality-informed risk prediction algorithms.

• Temporal causal models for clinical decision support.

• Benchmarking studies demonstrating improved robustness and interpretability.

Key Secondments

• Academic AI centre specialising in fairness analysis and explainability.

• Clinical cardiology environment supporting real-world validation.

Contribution to the Network

Provides core multimodal causal modelling methods used throughout the network.

DC3 – AI-ready clinical data and processing environments

Host: University medical centre with expertise in medical informatics and health-data infrastructures (WP2, WP3, WP4)

Objectives

• Assess organisational and technical AI readiness of healthcare environments.

• Co-design readiness frameworks with clinicians, IT professionals, patients and governance experts.

• Implement and evaluate a regulatory-compliant AI deployment pipeline.

Expected Results

• Data-readiness assessment framework.

• Infrastructure-readiness assessment framework.

• Guidelines for practical deployment of trustworthy healthcare AI.

• Open-source demonstrator environment.

Key Secondments

• Digital-health research centre specialising in health-data spaces and implementation science.

• Industrial AI environment focusing on explainability and uncertainty.

• Clinical implementation site enabling cross-institutional evaluation.

Contribution to the Network

Bridges AI development, governance and healthcare deployment.

DC4 – Sensitivity and uncertainty modelling for trustworthy AI

Host: Research and technology organisation with expertise in explainable AI and computational physiology (WP1, WP3, WP4)

Objectives

• Develop methods for quantifying prediction uncertainty and sensitivity.

• Create clinician-oriented confidence metrics.

• Evaluate the impact of uncertainty information on clinical decision-making.

Expected Results

• Integrated uncertainty and sensitivity framework.

• Calibration and robustness metrics.

• Evidence of improved interpretability and trust.

Key Secondments

• Academic centre specialising in explainable AI and evaluation methodologies.

• Medical-device company developing AI-enabled decision-support technologies.

• Clinical validation environment.

Contribution to the Network

Strengthens trustworthiness by making uncertainty explicit and clinically actionable.

DC5 – Privacy-preserving embedded AI for contactless physiological monitoring

Host: Technical university specialising in biomedical measurement technologies (WP2, WP4)

Objectives

• Analyse privacy and regulatory implications of contactless physiological monitoring.

• Develop distributed and privacy-preserving AI architectures.

• Evaluate privacy-performance trade-offs.

• Create privacy-by-design guidance for regulated medical technologies.

Expected Results

• Distributed privacy-preserving sensing platform.

• Benchmarking framework for privacy, efficiency and performance.

• Regulatory guidance for trustworthy embedded AI.

Key Secondments

• Clinical environment supporting physiological monitoring applications.

• Medical-device manufacturer developing advanced monitoring systems.

Contribution to the Network

Provides privacy-preserving deployment methodologies relevant to sensitive healthcare settings.

DC6 – Human-in-the-loop causal AI for physiological signals and medical imaging

Host: Technical university with expertise in explainable AI and biosignal analysis (WP1, WP3, WP4)

Objectives

• Design and evaluate human-in-the-loop AI paradigms.

• Strengthen transparency and user control.

• Improve safety and trust in clinical decision support.

Expected Results

• General human-in-the-loop framework.

• Multiple validated application demonstrators.

• Quantitative evidence regarding usability and trust.

Key Secondments

• Clinical medical-informatics environment.

• Emergency and intensive-care device manufacturer.

• Company specialising in long-term physiological monitoring technologies.

Contribution to the Network

Operationalises human oversight within trustworthy AI systems.

DC7 – Trustworthiness monitoring for digital health services

Host: University with expertise in digital health, health informatics and human- computer interaction (WP3, WP4)

Objectives

• Define continuous trustworthiness-monitoring methodologies.

• Design dashboards and monitoring tools.

• Assess clinical, organisational and economic impact at scale.

Expected Results

• Trustworthiness-monitoring framework.

• Monitoring dashboards and validation studies.

• Recommendations for large-scale deployment.

Key Secondments

• AI research laboratory supporting explainability and monitoring integration.

Contribution to the Network

Makes trustworthiness measurable throughout the AI lifecycle.

DC8 – Causal machine learning and counterfactual analysis for interventional medicine

Host: University research institute focusing on AI in cardiovascular medicine (WP1, WP2, WP4)

Objectives

• Investigate treatment-outcome confounding in interventional healthcare.

• Perform multicentre federated model development and evaluation.

• Develop counterfactual and sensitivity analysis methods.

Expected Results

• Causal multimodal prediction models.

• Multicentre evaluation framework.

• Open-source tools for explanation and counterfactual analysis.

Key Secondments

• University medical centre specialising in clinical data engineering and federated infrastructures.

• Clinical partner supporting implementation in routine practice.

Contribution to the Network

Demonstrates trustworthy causal AI in a high-impact interventional healthcare setting.

DC9 – Clinical adaptation and prognostic modelling for rare neurological disease

Host: Academic medical centre with expertise in digital health and rare-disease research (WP1, WP3, WP4)

Objectives

• Develop multimodal causal prognostic models.

• Identify causal connections among physiological, clinical and biomarker trajectories.

• Evaluate usability and clinical impact.

Expected Results

• Interpretable multimodal prognostic model.

• Benchmark dataset and validation framework.

• Clinical and regulatory evaluation report.

Key Secondments

• AI-driven cardiovascular medicine research institute.

• University medical centre supporting federated evaluation and workflow integration.

Contribution to the Network

Demonstrates transferability of trustworthy AI methodologies beyond cardiovascular medicine into complex neurological disease management.

Pertinence and innovative aspects of the research programme

Global health and policy roadmaps call for AI systems that are safe, interoperable and implementable in real-world healthcare environments. Yet adoption consistently stalls because of privacy concerns, interoperability challenges, bias, trust deficits and implementation barriers. PROJECT-X addresses these challenges through causal objectives, governance-ready engineering and healthcare-embedded validation, directly targeting gaps identified by healthcare-system stakeholders and implementation-science studies.

The programme responds to calls for organisation-wide strategies and enabling infrastructures capable of supporting trustworthy AI deployment beyond isolated research pilots. It also aligns with recent analyses emphasising resilience to variability, uncertainty and distribution shifts in healthcare data.

By embedding regulatory requirements such as AI governance frameworks, medical- device regulations, data-protection requirements and interoperability standards into the research process, the project goes beyond conventional AI prototypes and instead develops conformity-ready documentation, monitoring pipelines and implementation frameworks suitable for reuse by healthcare providers and industrial stakeholders.

Beyond the state of the art: scientific and technical innovations

The proposed innovations build upon and extend recent advances in causal explainability, federated learning, multimodal AI and trustworthy clinical decision support.

1. Causal, multimodal and federated AI

The programme develops multimodal causal models and federated transportability methodologies capable of supporting robust effect estimation across institutions.

The research integrates:

• longitudinal healthcare records,

• medical imaging,

• physiological measurements,

• biomarker information,

• patient-generated health data,

into semantically harmonised and privacy-preserving analytical frameworks.

Unlike classical predictive AI, the project explicitly considers transportability, identifiability and causal validity across heterogeneous clinical environments.

2. Resilient explainability and uncertainty quantification

The project develops novel methodologies for:

• sensitivity analysis,

• uncertainty quantification,

• counterfactual explainability,

• human-in-the-loop interactions.

These capabilities are integrated directly into explainable AI pipelines rather than added as post-processing components. Their purpose is to address reproducibility, robustness and trust limitations frequently reported in healthcare AI deployments.

3. Knowledge-augmented and physiology-aware models

The programme develops physiology-aware and knowledge-integrated AI architectures that incorporate formalised scientific and clinical knowledge into learning systems.

These approaches aim to:

• improve interpretability,

• improve out-of-distribution robustness,

• improve data efficiency,

• reduce model complexity,

• support deployment on constrained computing environments.

Such models directly address limitations of purely data-driven deep learning in healthcare applications.

Beyond the state of the art: clinical adaptation, governance and awareness

The programme deliberately moves beyond the traditional goal of producing incrementally better predictive models.

Instead, it develops a complete healthcare AI pathway, covering:

• algorithms,

• interoperability infrastructures,

• governance mechanisms,

• clinical adoption,

• regulatory readiness,

• implementation evaluation.

Key innovations include:

Healthcare-embedded validation

The programme performs healthcare-embedded case studies that progress from retrospective analyses toward shadow-mode and implementation-oriented evaluations.

Evaluation criteria include:

• diagnostic accuracy,

• workflow impact,

• time-to-decision,

• adoption indicators,

• implementation feasibility.

Stakeholder co-creation

The project systematically involves:

• clinicians,

• patients,

• data stewards,

• healthcare organisations,

• regulatory stakeholders,

through co-design activities intended to address adoption barriers such as:

• organisational resistance,

• workflow disruption,

• trust concerns,

• perceived unfairness,

• transparency requirements.

Regulatory science integration

The programme integrates legal, regulatory and implementation expertise to produce:

• regulatory-aligned documentation,

• monitoring frameworks,

• impact-assessment methodologies,

• implementation guidance.

These outputs are intended to support future standardisation and policy-development activities.

Positioning versus existing doctoral programmes

Many existing doctoral programmes in AI and digital health focus predominantly on:

• algorithms,

• data infrastructures,

• ethics,

• management.

Few programmes integrate all of these dimensions into a single coherent framework.

PROJECT-X distinguishes itself through three characteristics:

Four-pillar architecture

The programme is organised around:

1. Trustworthiness

2. Interoperability

3. Awareness

4. Clinical adaptation

This common framework links all doctoral projects and training activities.

Regulatory integration by design

Regulatory and governance requirements are embedded directly into research questions, infrastructures and evaluation strategies instead of being treated as downstream compliance activities.

Combination of causal AI and real-world implementation

The programme combines:

• advanced causal machine learning,

• healthcare implementation science,

• interoperability research,

• human-centred design,

• health-economic evaluation,

within a single doctoral training environment.

This combination addresses a recognised shortage of specialists capable of simultaneously understanding:

• causal modelling,

• healthcare workflows,

• data governance,

• validation methodologies,

• regulatory compliance.

Expected transformation

By the end of the programme, the consortium will deliver:

1. Reference methodologies for causal estimation, explainability, uncertainty analysis and sensitivity assessment.

2. Interoperable and privacy-preserving data and computation frameworks.

3. A new generation of researchers trained at the intersection of AI, healthcare and governance.

4. Demonstrated clinical adaptation workflows supported by implementation and compliance frameworks.

Collectively, these outputs establish a blueprint for regulation-aligned causal AI in healthcare, moving beyond predictive modelling toward safe, trustworthy and effective decision-support systems suitable for real-world deployment.

--- 1.2 | Soundness of the proposed methodology ---
Overall methodology

We adopt a highly interdisciplinary and strongly collaborative approach that prioritises early and open exchange of ideas within the consortium and with the wider community.

Our overarching ambition is to replace correlation-driven pipelines with causal AI systems that are resilient to real-world data challenges, interoperable across heterogeneous healthcare infrastructures and regulatory compliant.

The programme balances fundamental research with applied validation in healthcare environments, ensuring that methods remain theoretically rigorous, technically auditable and practically implementable in routine healthcare.

This framework is underpinned by four methodological advances.

Causal AI and counterfactual reasoning

Instead of relying solely on black-box prediction, the programme develops models capable of estimating cause-effect relationships and counterfactual outcomes.

The models explicitly encode assumptions and quantify both structural and statistical uncertainty.

This directly addresses important reproducibility, robustness and bias challenges identified in healthcare AI.

Regulatory-grade pipelines

Compliance with healthcare AI regulations and governance frameworks is treated as a methodological requirement rather than a post hoc constraint.

Risk classification, transparency, robustness, human oversight and lifecycle monitoring are embedded throughout the development process within a quality-managed framework.

The methodology operationalises major regulatory requirements relevant to high-risk healthcare AI systems, including medical-device, data-governance and AI-governance obligations.

Federated and privacy-preserving interoperability

The programme leverages federated learning, split learning, standardised healthcare data models and selection-diagram methodologies to transform identifiability and privacy into engineering problems.

This directly addresses long-standing interoperability and data-sharing barriers present in healthcare IT ecosystems.

The approach seeks to ensure that privacy preservation, semantic interoperability and model validity are jointly addressed rather than treated as independent challenges.

Healthcare-embedded implementation and co-creation

Healthcare case studies are designed in close collaboration with:

• clinicians,

• healthcare IT professionals,

• patients,

• healthcare organisations,

• regulatory stakeholders.

This enables the programme to address organisational, ethical and workflow barriers that frequently hinder AI adoption.

Together, these methodological pillars address the principal barriers limiting healthcare AI impact:

• data quality,

• interoperability,

• transparency,

• trust,

• governance,

• regulation,

• implementation.

The resulting closed-loop methodology follows the sequence:

Causal Question

↓

Identifiability Analysis

↓

Federated Data Preparation

↓

Model Development

↓

Clinical Evaluation

↓

Assurance & Documentation

and is consistently applied across all research projects and healthcare use cases.

Integration of methods and disciplines to pursue the objectives

Achieving the objectives requires integration of technical, clinical, regulatory and social- science disciplines.

Computer science and causal inference

Development of novel algorithms for:

• robust training,

• sensitivity analysis,

• counterfactual evaluation,

• fairness-aware learning,

grounded in modern causal-inference and trustworthy-AI research.

Biomedical and clinical sciences

Validation of models within cardiovascular and related healthcare domains ensures that:

• causal graphs,

• estimands,

• predictions,

• recommendations

reflect clinically meaningful mechanisms and healthcare-relevant endpoints.

This addresses the scarcity of rigorously evaluated healthcare implementation studies.

Regulatory science and legal expertise

The methodology aligns with:

• healthcare AI regulations,

• medical-device requirements,

• interoperability obligations,

• data-protection regulations.

Research activities include co-development of:

• conformity-ready documentation,

• risk-management artefacts,

• monitoring protocols,

• compliance assessment methodologies.

Social sciences and human-factors research

The methodology incorporates:

• participatory design,

• organisational-change models,

• human-centred assessment,

• ethical evaluation.

Trust, usability and perceived fairness are explicitly evaluated as measurable outcomes rather than secondary effects.

Interdisciplinarity embedded across work packages

Interdisciplinarity is built directly into the work-package structure.

Trustworthiness work package

Combines:

• machine learning,

• statistics,

• ethics,

• explainability,

• causal reasoning.

Interoperability work package

Combines:

• health informatics,

• systems engineering,

• privacy technologies,

• legal compliance.

Awareness work package

Combines:

• human-centred design,

• training sciences,

• stakeholder engagement,

• adoption science.

Clinical adaptation work package

Combines:

• biomedical sciences,

• implementation science,

• organisational change,

• regulatory evaluation.

The same interdisciplinary integration is reflected within individual doctoral projects.

Examples include:

• causal machine learning integrated with clinical decision support,

• AI-readiness assessment combining informatics and regulatory science,

• human-in-the-loop AI combined with social-science approaches to trust and adoption,

• disease-specific clinical applications combined with federated learning and causal inference.

These projects collectively exemplify interdisciplinary collaboration in healthcare AI.

Gender dimension and diversity aspects

Sex, gender and additional diversity characteristics are treated as scientific variables.

These variables are incorporated throughout model development and evaluation:

• represented in causal structures as potential causes, effects or mediators,

• included within datasets whenever available,

• analysed via subgroup performance assessments,

• monitored through calibration and error analysis,

• incorporated into bias-detection and mitigation workflows.

Human-centred design activities involve diverse groups of clinicians and patients to ensure that explanations and decisions remain understandable and trustworthy across populations.

Integration of diversity considerations strengthens:

• validity,

• robustness,

• fairness,

• generalisability.

Open science practices

Open science is implemented within the constraints imposed by medical-data protection and high-risk AI governance.

All publications will be open access wherever possible.

A data-management strategy ensures adherence to FAIR principles through:

• standard ontologies,

• persistent identifiers,

• machine-readable metadata,

• reproducible workflows,

• documentation standards.

The programme intends to release, where legally and ethically feasible:

• generic algorithms,

• benchmarking frameworks,

• software components,

• synthetic datasets.

Key findings will be disseminated through:

• publications,

• preprints,

• analysis plans,

• reusable software assets.

The guiding principle throughout the project is:

As open as possible, as closed as necessary.

--- 1.3 | Quality and credibility of the training programme ---
1.3.1 Overview and content structure of the doctoral training programme

The training programme equips doctoral candidates with the integrated expertise needed to design, evaluate and deploy causal AI systems in real clinical and regulatory environments, while systematically integrating transferable skills, inter- and multidisciplinary content, and intersectoral exposure in line with the MSCA “triple-i” principles.

Current doctoral training in AI and digital health primarily focuses on predictive modelling and technical implementation. Only a limited number of programmes address causal inference, clinical evaluation and compliance with evolving European frameworks, such as the AI Act, the Medical Device Regulation (MDR), and the European Health Data Space (EHDS), in an integrated way.

The Doctoral Network (DN) provides a structured training framework that combines:

1. Individual research and local doctoral training at the host institution, including enrolment in an accredited PhD programme and discipline-specific coursework;

2. Network-wide scientific and transferable skills training, delivered through dedicated schools, workshops and online modules; and

3. Intersectoral and international secondments in hospitals, industry and regulatory/standardisation bodies, where candidates apply causal AI methods in real-world health settings.

This architecture is implemented and monitored via the Training and Career Development work package and the Training Programme Coordination task in the management work package.

Together, local doctoral-school provision and the network-wide programme form a single, coherent curriculum: each DC’s Personal Career Development Plan (PCDP) maps how local and network-wide activities, including secondments, contribute to TG1– TG6 and to the four programme pillars (trustworthiness, interoperability, awareness, clinical adaptation).

1.3.2 Training objectives and stakeholder needs

The training programme is guided by the following network-wide objectives, which were developed in dialogue with the network's key stakeholder groups (including university hospitals, technology and data providers, SMEs, policy and standardization bodies) and are reflected in the individual DC project descriptions and work package training goals:

TG1 – Core scientific skills in causal and trustworthy AI for health

DCs will develop an in-depth understanding of causal modelling, counterfactual reasoning, transportability and identifiability, sensitivity and uncertainty analysis, fairness and robustness, multimodal data fusion and interoperable implementation in clinical contexts.

TG2 – Clinical, biomedical and public health literacy

DCs will develop comprehensive expertise in cardiovascular and related clinical domains, as well as in study design, outcomes, care pathways and health system constraints. This expertise will enable them to collaborate with healthcare professionals in defining clinically meaningful estimands and interpreting model outputs.

TG3 – Data governance, regulation and ethics

Training covers GDPR and health data governance, EU AI Act requirements for high-risk medical AI systems, MDR/IVDR interfaces, the European Health Data Space, research integrity and responsible research and innovation (RRI), as well as patient and right- holder perspectives.

TG4 – Transferable and complementary skills

In line with MSCA guidance and the European Competence Framework for Researchers, DCs will develop competencies in project management, teamwork, leadership, intercultural collaboration, scientific writing and communication, stakeholder engagement, open science, and teaching and mentoring.

TG5 – Innovation, entrepreneurship and impact

DCs will learn how to translate research into innovation, including IPR management, standardization, needs and market analysis, and co-creation with industry, hospitals and public bodies.

TG6 – Career development and resilience

DCs will be prepared for diverse careers in academia, hospitals, industry, regulatory agencies and public administration through targeted career-development training, structured exposure to non-academic environments, and mentoring.

These six training objectives (TG1–TG6) are operationalized through the integrated training architecture and triple-i implementation described in Section 1.3.3.

Each training objective (TG1–TG6) directly supports specific components of the research programme: TGs 1–3 align with methodological WPs 1–3, TG2 reinforces clinical adaptations, TG4 supports management activities, and TG5–6 underpin the impact, innovation and career-development goals embedded in the training and impact work packages.

1.3.3 Triple-I approach

The programme implements a systematic, cross-cutting “triple-i” approach to achieve TG1–TG6:

International

All projects involve cross-border recruitment and at least one international secondment. Network-wide events rotate between countries and are streamed or recorded to maximize accessibility. DCs are encouraged and supported to present at international conferences and participate in international research networks.

Intersectoral

Secondments and co-supervision connect universities with university hospitals, digital health SMEs, and other non-academic partners. DCs gain first-hand experience of clinical workflows, regulatory compliance processes and product-development lifecycles, which fosters a shared language between themselves, clinicians and regulators.

Interdisciplinary

Each DC is exposed to computer science, statistics, medicine, law/regulation and human-centred design/social sciences through joint courses, co-supervision and cross- work-package collaborations, reflecting the sociotechnical nature of trustworthy causal AI in healthcare.

1.3.4 Special training elements of the network

Local training at host organizations

Each host institution provides structured doctoral training through its graduate or doctoral school. This training includes core scientific courses and seminars, as well as modules on transferable skills such as research ethics, gender and diversity, and open science. Wherever possible, these courses are made available on-site or online to DCs from other beneficiary institutions, thereby increasing efficiency and coherence. Individual research projects, group meetings, journal clubs, and local clinical seminars ensure that DCs are fully integrated into vibrant research and clinical environments.

Network-wide training

Non-academic partners lead or co-lead sessions on clinical workflows, regulatory compliance, entrepreneurship and innovation management, ensuring that intersectoral exposure is substantive and aligned with stakeholder needs. These activities, with indicative timing and contributions of beneficiaries and associated partners, are listed in Table 1.

Table 1. Main Network-Wide Training Events, Conferences and Contribution of Beneficiaries

1. Kick-Start training week organised by the coordinating institution

Day 1 (TG1–2): public lectures from invited European and international experts and consortium partners on topics such as translational health research, biomedical device development, wearable monitoring, cardiovascular disorders, signal processing, model- based AI, medical imaging, mobile health and explainable AI.

Day 2 (TG4–5): project, scientific and training-goal overview, theoretical and practical introductions, industry session.

Day 3 (TG4–5–6): transferable skills course and career planning; scientific communication and presentation skills; open-science basics with a focus on research- data management (RDM), FAIR principles, ethics and research integrity.

Day 4 (TG5): poster session and laboratory visits.

2. Summer School for “Succeeding in my PhD Journey”

• Pre-assignments: personal study-plan draft, career scenarios (TG6)

• Visiting professors, former MSCA alumni career stories, groupwork (TG4)

• Post-assignments: PCDP completion, groupwork (TG6)

3. Training on ethics and regulations for AI in healthcare

Day 1 (TG3): tutorials on EU regulations and ethics, and their implications for healthcare AI models.

Day 2 (TG1–3): privacy challenges, data protection, split-learning and federated-AI methodologies.

Day 3 (TG5): how to translate scientific results into innovation, including the pathway from research to product development.

4. Training on interoperability standards for clinical AI models

Day 1 (TG3): public lectures from invited international experts and consortium partners on interoperability standards.

Day 2 (TG3): semantic and syntactic metadata standards for AI models.

Day 3 (TG2–5): integrating large-scale data and explainable AI into daily clinical practice; hospital and data-centre visits; lectures on regulatory standards.

5. International minisymposium on Trustworthy AI for Healthcare

The consortium will organise a dedicated minisymposium on trustworthy AI for healthcare at major international conferences. The event will feature scientific presentations by doctoral fellows and supervisors, showcasing project results to a global audience. The minisymposium will foster networking with international experts, enhance collaboration opportunities, and increase the project’s impact, visibility and scientific reach.

6. Course on AI and Cardiovascular Health

Day 1 (TG4–6): clinical decision-support tools empowered by AI.

Day 2 (TG1–4–6): role and impact of trustworthy, causal and explainable AI principles in cardiology.

Day 3 (TG4–5): unlocking insights from cardiology data using AI and exploring opportunities for human-AI collaboration.

7. Final International Conference on Trustworthy AI for Healthcare

Day 1 (TG1–2): public lecture on translating AI research into clinical practice; invited lectures.

Day 2–3 (TG1–2–5): scientific talks by fellows and contributed talks by external participants.

Day 4 (TG4–6): focus session on future collaborations and sustainability beyond project duration; networking and institutional visits.

1.4.2 Quality of supervision for DN

Supervision in the DN is organised around a multi-layered structure that combines day- to-day guidance at the host institution with network-wide monitoring and support:

• Each DC has a main academic supervisor at the recruiting beneficiary and at least one co-supervisor or mentor from another sector (hospital, SME or other non-academic partner). Where appropriate, an additional mentor from a complementary discipline (e.g. law/regulation, human-centred design) is included. Together, they form an Individual Training Panel (ITP) or supervisory committee.

• Within the first three months, the ITP and DC jointly agree a Personal Career Development Plan (PCDP), specifying research objectives, training needs, secondments, open-science commitments and career goals. The PCDP is reviewed at least every six months and updated when needed; key milestones are aligned with host doctoral-school requirements and network deliverables, and PCDP updates are validated through the Supervisory Board as part of training monitoring activities.

Day-to-day supervision follows a clear and consistent policy across the consortium:

• Regular meetings between DCs and their main supervisors (typically every 2–4 weeks) focus on scientific progress, skills development and well-being.

• ITP meetings (in person or online) are held at least twice per year, often aligned with network-wide events, to review PCDPs, training progress, secondment planning and career perspectives.

• Supervisors operate an open-door communication culture, encouraging DCs to raise scientific or personal concerns early. Short ad hoc meetings and online interactions complement formal supervision sessions and provide a two-way feedback channel.

Progress and review procedures are embedded in project governance:

• The Supervisory Board (SB) oversees the overall supervision strategy and ensures that PCDPs, secondments and training objectives are implemented consistently across sites, in line with the MSCA Guidelines on Supervision.

• Training and supervision quality are monitored through annual progress reports, PCDP updates and anonymous feedback questionnaires completed by DCs after major training events.

• Clear procedures for conflict prevention and resolution are included in the Consortium Agreement (e.g. two-step escalation from local resolution within the ITP to intervention by the SB and, if needed, an external ombudsperson), ensuring that problems can be addressed in a timely and confidential manner.

Supervision explicitly includes career development, integration and well-being. DCs are supported in building professional networks (e.g. conference participation, joint publications, involvement in standards or guideline activities) and are encouraged to co- supervise MSc students or contribute to teaching, under guidance. Integration into local research and clinical groups is fostered through lab meetings, journal clubs and clinical seminars, ensuring that each DC works within a vibrant environment rather than in isolation.

Although the project is a standard Doctoral Network (not an Industrial Doctorate or Joint Doctorate scheme), each DC benefits from this structured co-supervision team, which provides complementary intersectoral and interdisciplinary guidance comparable in quality to mandatory joint-supervision schemes in industrial and joint doctorates.

--- 1.1 | Quality and pertinence of the project’s research and innovation objectives (and the extent to which they are ambitious, and go beyond the state of the art) ---
Introduction, objectives and overview of the overall research programme

Despite rapid advances, the current state of AI in healthcare remains correlation-driven, fragmented and poorly adapted to clinical reality. Most deployed models operate as statistical predictors rather than decision technologies and therefore struggle with external validity, transportability and regulatory acceptance. Systematic reviews confirm that adoption is slowed by fragmented data environments, limited explainability and a lack of prospective clinical evidence. In cardiovascular applications, the literature reveals broad enthusiasm but few implementation case studies and no clear pathways for compliance with emerging AI regulations. This leaves hospitals, regulators and patients with "AI as a promise" rather than a demonstrably safe and auditable intervention tool.

The proposal is timely because emerging regulatory and policy frameworks now require trustworthy, explainable and interoperable AI in high-risk healthcare settings. PROJECT-X directly responds to these policy drivers while contributing to broader digital-health and societal objectives through fair, robust AI tools that are clinically actionable across diverse populations.

PROJECT-X’s overarching ambition is:

1. to replace correlation-centric models with causal objectives and counterfactual evaluation;

2. to treat interoperability and governance as first-class design constraints;

3. to embed human-in-the-loop co-creation and targeted stakeholder training;

4. to execute healthcare-embedded case studies that generate evidence on safety, adoption and value.

Together, these elements define a cohesive research programme addressing key skills and knowledge gaps in healthcare AI.

Specific measurable research and innovation objectives

O1 – Trustworthy causal AI (WP1)

Develop explainable, fair and sensitivity-aware causal AI models that articulate assumptions, quantify uncertainty and provide counterfactual “what-if” and cause- effect reasoning at both patient and policy levels.

Success KPIs

• KPI1.1: ≥1 multimodal AI model integrated with causal modules.

• KPI1.2: ≥10 clinicians test the tool and ≥80% report improved confidence in AI- supported decisions.

• KPI1.3: ≥1 joint report or white paper citing causal evidence generated within the project.

O2 – Interoperability for identifiability (WP2)

Establish multimodal, robust and privacy-preserving data flows and the semantic structures required by target causal graphs.

Implement federated identifiability and transportability checks across sites to ensure that models remain valid, generalisable and clinically deployable under heterogeneous real-world conditions.

Success KPIs

• KPI2.1: successful integration of ≥4 data modalities into a unified semantic schema.

• KPI2.2: ≥1 pilot model per use case integrating ≥3 formalised clinical or physiological rules.

• KPI2.3: ≥1 data exchange protocol between academic and industrial partners.

• KPI2.4: ≥1 published guideline or white paper reviewed by technical, clinical and regulatory stakeholders.

O3 – Awareness and co-creation (WP3)

Deliver role-specific training for clinicians, data stewards and regulators; implement human-in-the-loop AI tools; and co-create interfaces with patients to improve usability, trust and real-world alignment.

Success KPIs

• KPI3.1: clinician and patient usability ratings ≥80%.

• KPI3.2: ≥2 co-design workshops with ≥15 participants.

• KPI3.3: ≥3 AI tools supporting interactive clinician feedback and retraining mechanisms.

O4 – Clinical adaptation and evidence (WP4)

Translate AI-based decision support into healthcare practice by identifying practical barriers to deployment.

Conduct retrospective evaluations across:

• Rare Neurodegenerative Cohorts

• Structural Heart Intervention Cohorts

• Heart Failure Cohorts

• population-level studies

• routine clinical workflows

Success KPIs

• KPI4.1: ≥1 health-economic or cost-effectiveness evaluation.

• KPI4.2: ≥2 policy briefs or white papers.

• KPI4.3: implementation of at least one AI system in an additional clinical environment.

Cross-cutting objective (CO)

Operationalise relevant AI regulations and best-practice guidelines across all objectives by embedding:

• transparency

• risk classification

• robustness

• human oversight

• lifecycle monitoring

throughout model development and deployment.

Success KPIs

• Unified compliance and risk-management framework.

• ≥1 regulatory-readiness toolkit publication.

• Dissemination through at least two international channels.

DC1 – Physiology-aware AI for clinical decision support

Host: Research-intensive European university with expertise in biomedical signal processing and explainable AI (WP1, WP2, WP4)

Objectives

• Formalise clinical and physiological knowledge including heuristics, rules, causal relations and constraints for cardiovascular use cases.

• Develop compact physiology-aware AI architectures that integrate domain knowledge at data, model and decision levels.

Expected Results

• Demonstration of improved robustness and generalisability compared with black-box baselines.

• Reusable modules supporting explainability and trustworthy AI across the network.

Provides the physiological and mechanistic foundations supporting trustworthiness, interoperability and clinical adaptation.

Provides core multimodal causal modelling methods used throughout the network.

Contribution to the Network

Bridges AI development, governance and healthcare deployment.

Host: Research and technology organisation with expertise in explainable AI and computational physiology (WP1, WP3, WP4)

Objectives

Strengthens trustworthiness by making uncertainty explicit and clinically actionable.

Host: Technical university with expertise in explainable AI and biosignal analysis (WP1, WP3, WP4)

Objectives

Operationalises human oversight within trustworthy AI systems.

Host: University with expertise in digital health, health informatics and human- computer interaction (WP3, WP4)

Objectives

Makes trustworthiness measurable throughout the AI lifecycle.

Host: University research institute focusing on AI in cardiovascular medicine (WP1, WP2, WP4)

Objectives

• Perform multicentre federated model development and evaluation.

Expected Results

Demonstrates trustworthy causal AI in a high-impact interventional healthcare setting.

Host: Academic medical centre with expertise in digital health and rare-disease research (WP1, WP3, WP4)

• Evaluate usability and clinical impact.

Expected Results

• Benchmark dataset and validation framework.

• Clinical and regulatory evaluation report.

Key Secondments

• AI-driven cardiovascular medicine research institute.

• University medical centre supporting federated evaluation and workflow integration.

Contribution to the Network

Demonstrates transferability of trustworthy AI methodologies beyond cardiovascular medicine into complex neurological disease management.

Pertinence and innovative aspects of the research programme

Global health and policy roadmaps call for AI systems that are safe, interoperable and implementable in real-world healthcare environments. Yet adoption consistently stalls because of privacy concerns, interoperability challenges, bias, trust deficits and implementation barriers. PROJECT-X addresses these challenges through causal objectives, governance-ready engineering and healthcare-embedded validation, directly targeting gaps identified by healthcare-system stakeholders and implementation-science studies.

The programme responds to calls for organisation-wide strategies and enabling infrastructures capable of supporting trustworthy AI deployment beyond isolated research pilots. It also aligns with recent analyses emphasising resilience to variability, uncertainty and distribution shifts in healthcare data.

By embedding regulatory requirements such as AI governance frameworks, medical- device regulations, data-protection requirements and interoperability standards into the research process, the project goes beyond conventional AI prototypes and instead develops conformity-ready documentation, monitoring pipelines and implementation frameworks suitable for reuse by healthcare providers and industrial stakeholders.

Beyond the state of the art: scientific and technical innovations

The proposed innovations build upon and extend recent advances in causal explainability, federated learning, multimodal AI and trustworthy clinical decision support.

1. Causal, multimodal and federated AI

The programme develops multimodal causal models and federated transportability methodologies capable of supporting robust effect estimation across institutions.

The research integrates:

• longitudinal healthcare records,

• medical imaging,

• physiological measurements,

• biomarker information,

• patient-generated health data,

into semantically harmonised and privacy-preserving analytical frameworks.

Unlike classical predictive AI, the project explicitly considers transportability, identifiability and causal validity across heterogeneous clinical environments.

2. Resilient explainability and uncertainty quantification

The project develops novel methodologies for:

• sensitivity analysis,

• uncertainty quantification,

• counterfactual explainability,

• human-in-the-loop interactions.

These capabilities are integrated directly into explainable AI pipelines rather than added as post-processing components. Their purpose is to address reproducibility, robustness and trust limitations frequently reported in healthcare AI deployments.

3. Knowledge-augmented and physiology-aware models

The programme develops physiology-aware and knowledge-integrated AI architectures that incorporate formalised scientific and clinical knowledge into learning systems.

These approaches aim to:

• improve interpretability,

• improve out-of-distribution robustness,

• improve data efficiency,

• reduce model complexity,

• support deployment on constrained computing environments.

Such models directly address limitations of purely data-driven deep learning in healthcare applications.

Beyond the state of the art: clinical adaptation, governance and awareness

The programme deliberately moves beyond the traditional goal of producing incrementally better predictive models.

Instead, it develops a complete healthcare AI pathway, covering:

• algorithms,

• interoperability infrastructures,

• governance mechanisms,

• clinical adoption,

• regulatory readiness,

• implementation evaluation.

Key innovations include:

Healthcare-embedded validation

The programme performs healthcare-embedded case studies that progress from retrospective analyses toward shadow-mode and implementation-oriented evaluations.

Evaluation criteria include:

• diagnostic accuracy,

• workflow impact,

• time-to-decision,

• adoption indicators,

• implementation feasibility.

Stakeholder co-creation

The project systematically involves:

• clinicians,

• patients,

• data stewards,

• healthcare organisations,

• regulatory stakeholders,

through co-design activities intended to address adoption barriers such as:

• organisational resistance,

• workflow disruption,

• trust concerns,

• perceived unfairness,

• transparency requirements.

Regulatory science integration

The programme integrates legal, regulatory and implementation expertise to produce:

• regulatory-aligned documentation,

• monitoring frameworks,

• impact-assessment methodologies,

• implementation guidance.

These outputs are intended to support future standardisation and policy-development activities.

Positioning versus existing doctoral programmes

Many existing doctoral programmes in AI and digital health focus predominantly on:

• algorithms,

• data infrastructures,

• ethics,

• management.

Few programmes integrate all of these dimensions into a single coherent framework.

PROJECT-X distinguishes itself through three characteristics:

Four-pillar architecture

The programme is organised around:

1. Trustworthiness

2. Interoperability

3. Awareness

4. Clinical adaptation

This common framework links all doctoral projects and training activities.

Regulatory integration by design

Regulatory and governance requirements are embedded directly into research questions, infrastructures and evaluation strategies instead of being treated as downstream compliance activities.

Combination of causal AI and real-world implementation

The programme combines:

• advanced causal machine learning,

• healthcare implementation science,

• interoperability research,

• human-centred design,

• health-economic evaluation,

within a single doctoral training environment.

This combination addresses a recognised shortage of specialists capable of simultaneously understanding:

• causal modelling,

• healthcare workflows,

• data governance,

• validation methodologies,

• regulatory compliance.

Expected transformation

By the end of the programme, the consortium will deliver:

1. Reference methodologies for causal estimation, explainability, uncertainty analysis and sensitivity assessment.

2. Interoperable and privacy-preserving data and computation frameworks.

3. A new generation of researchers trained at the intersection of AI, healthcare and governance.

4. Demonstrated clinical adaptation workflows supported by implementation and compliance frameworks.

Collectively, these outputs establish a blueprint for regulation-aligned causal AI in healthcare, moving beyond predictive modelling toward safe, trustworthy and effective decision-support systems suitable for real-world deployment.

--- 1.2 | Soundness of the proposed methodology ---
Overall methodology

We adopt a highly interdisciplinary and strongly collaborative approach that prioritises early and open exchange of ideas within the consortium and with the wider community.

Our overarching ambition is to replace correlation-driven pipelines with causal AI systems that are resilient to real-world data challenges, interoperable across heterogeneous healthcare infrastructures and regulatory compliant.

The programme balances fundamental research with applied validation in healthcare environments, ensuring that methods remain theoretically rigorous, technically auditable and practically implementable in routine healthcare.

This framework is underpinned by four methodological advances.

Causal AI and counterfactual reasoning

Instead of relying solely on black-box prediction, the programme develops models capable of estimating cause-effect relationships and counterfactual outcomes.

The models explicitly encode assumptions and quantify both structural and statistical uncertainty.

This directly addresses important reproducibility, robustness and bias challenges identified in healthcare AI.

Regulatory-grade pipelines

Compliance with healthcare AI regulations and governance frameworks is treated as a methodological requirement rather than a post hoc constraint.

Risk classification, transparency, robustness, human oversight and lifecycle monitoring are embedded throughout the development process within a quality-managed framework.

The methodology operationalises major regulatory requirements relevant to high-risk healthcare AI systems, including medical-device, data-governance and AI-governance obligations.

Federated and privacy-preserving interoperability

The programme leverages federated learning, split learning, standardised healthcare data models and selection-diagram methodologies to transform identifiability and privacy into engineering problems.

This directly addresses long-standing interoperability and data-sharing barriers present in healthcare IT ecosystems.

The approach seeks to ensure that privacy preservation, semantic interoperability and model validity are jointly addressed rather than treated as independent challenges.

Healthcare-embedded implementation and co-creation

Healthcare case studies are designed in close collaboration with:

• clinicians,

• healthcare IT professionals,

• patients,

• healthcare organisations,

• regulatory stakeholders.

This enables the programme to address organisational, ethical and workflow barriers that frequently hinder AI adoption.

Together, these methodological pillars address the principal barriers limiting healthcare AI impact:

• data quality,

• interoperability,

• transparency,

• trust,

• governance,

• regulation,

• implementation.

The resulting closed-loop methodology follows the sequence:

Causal Question

↓

Identifiability Analysis

↓

Federated Data Preparation

↓

Model Development

↓

Clinical Evaluation

↓

Assurance & Documentation

and is consistently applied across all research projects and healthcare use cases.

Integration of methods and disciplines to pursue the objectives

Achieving the objectives requires integration of technical, clinical, regulatory and social- science disciplines.

Computer science and causal inference

Development of novel algorithms for:

• robust training,

• sensitivity analysis,

• counterfactual evaluation,

• fairness-aware learning,

grounded in modern causal-inference and trustworthy-AI research.

Biomedical and clinical sciences

Validation of models within cardiovascular and related healthcare domains ensures that:

• causal graphs,

• estimands,

• predictions,

• recommendations

reflect clinically meaningful mechanisms and healthcare-relevant endpoints.

This addresses the scarcity of rigorously evaluated healthcare implementation studies.

Regulatory science and legal expertise

The methodology aligns with:

• healthcare AI regulations,

• medical-device requirements,

• interoperability obligations,

• data-protection regulations.

Research activities include co-development of:

• conformity-ready documentation,

• risk-management artefacts,

• monitoring protocols,

• compliance assessment methodologies.

Social sciences and human-factors research

The methodology incorporates:

• participatory design,

• organisational-change models,

• human-centred assessment,

• ethical evaluation.

Trust, usability and perceived fairness are explicitly evaluated as measurable outcomes rather than secondary effects.

Interdisciplinarity embedded across work packages

Trustworthiness work package

Examples include:

• human-in-the-loop AI combined with social-science approaches to trust and adoption,

These projects collectively exemplify interdisciplinary collaboration in healthcare AI.

Gender dimension and diversity aspects

Sex, gender and additional diversity characteristics are treated as scientific variables.

These variables are incorporated throughout model development and evaluation:

• represented in causal structures as potential causes, effects or mediators,

• included within datasets whenever available,

• analysed via subgroup performance assessments,

• monitored through calibration and error analysis,

• incorporated into bias-detection and mitigation workflows.

Human-centred design activities involve diverse groups of clinicians and patients to ensure that explanations and decisions remain understandable and trustworthy across populations.

Integration of diversity considerations strengthens:

• validity,

• robustness,

• fairness,

• generalisability.

Open science practices

Open science is implemented within the constraints imposed by medical-data protection and high-risk AI governance.

All publications will be open access wherever possible.

A data-management strategy ensures adherence to FAIR principles through:

• standard ontologies,

• persistent identifiers,

• machine-readable metadata,

• reproducible workflows,

• benchmarking frameworks,

• software components,

As open as possible, as closed as necessary.

--- 1.3 | Quality and credibility of the training programme ---
1.3.1 Overview and content structure of the doctoral training programme

The training programme equips doctoral candidates with the integrated expertise needed to design, evaluate and deploy causal AI systems in real clinical and regulatory environments, while systematically integrating transferable skills, inter- and multidisciplinary content, and intersectoral exposure in line with the MSCA “triple-i” principles.

Current doctoral training in AI and digital health primarily focuses on predictive modelling and technical implementation. Only a limited number of programmes address causal inference, clinical evaluation and compliance with evolving European frameworks, such as the AI Act, the Medical Device Regulation (MDR), and the European Health Data Space (EHDS), in an integrated way.

The Doctoral Network (DN) provides a structured training framework that combines:

1. Individual research and local doctoral training at the host institution, including enrolment in an accredited PhD programme and discipline-specific coursework;

2. Network-wide scientific and transferable skills training, delivered through dedicated schools, workshops and online modules; and

3. Intersectoral and international secondments in hospitals, industry and regulatory/standardisation bodies, where candidates apply causal AI methods in real-world health settings.

This architecture is implemented and monitored via the Training and Career Development work package and the Training Programme Coordination task in the management work package.

Together, local doctoral-school provision and the network-wide programme form a single, coherent curriculum: each DC’s Personal Career Development Plan (PCDP) maps how local and network-wide activities, including secondments, contribute to TG1– TG6 and to the four programme pillars (trustworthiness, interoperability, awareness, clinical adaptation).

1.3.2 Training objectives and stakeholder needs

The training programme is guided by the following network-wide objectives, which were developed in dialogue with the network's key stakeholder groups (including university hospitals, technology and data providers, SMEs, policy and standardization bodies) and are reflected in the individual DC project descriptions and work package training goals:

TG1 – Core scientific skills in causal and trustworthy AI for health

DCs will develop an in-depth understanding of causal modelling, counterfactual reasoning, transportability and identifiability, sensitivity and uncertainty analysis, fairness and robustness, multimodal data fusion and interoperable implementation in clinical contexts.

TG2 – Clinical, biomedical and public health literacy

DCs will develop comprehensive expertise in cardiovascular and related clinical domains, as well as in study design, outcomes, care pathways and health system constraints. This expertise will enable them to collaborate with healthcare professionals in defining clinically meaningful estimands and interpreting model outputs.

TG3 – Data governance, regulation and ethics

Training covers GDPR and health data governance, EU AI Act requirements for high-risk medical AI systems, MDR/IVDR interfaces, the European Health Data Space, research integrity and responsible research and innovation (RRI), as well as patient and right- holder perspectives.

TG4 – Transferable and complementary skills

In line with MSCA guidance and the European Competence Framework for Researchers, DCs will develop competencies in project management, teamwork, leadership, intercultural collaboration, scientific writing and communication, stakeholder engagement, open science, and teaching and mentoring.

TG5 – Innovation, entrepreneurship and impact

DCs will learn how to translate research into innovation, including IPR management, standardization, needs and market analysis, and co-creation with industry, hospitals and public bodies.

TG6 – Career development and resilience

DCs will be prepared for diverse careers in academia, hospitals, industry, regulatory agencies and public administration through targeted career-development training, structured exposure to non-academic environments, and mentoring.

These six training objectives (TG1–TG6) are operationalized through the integrated training architecture and triple-i implementation described in Section 1.3.3.

Each training objective (TG1–TG6) directly supports specific components of the research programme: TGs 1–3 align with methodological WPs 1–3, TG2 reinforces clinical adaptations, TG4 supports management activities, and TG5–6 underpin the impact, innovation and career-development goals embedded in the training and impact work packages.

1.3.3 Triple-I approach

The programme implements a systematic, cross-cutting “triple-i” approach to achieve TG1–TG6:

International

All projects involve cross-border recruitment and at least one international secondment. Network-wide events rotate between countries and are streamed or recorded to maximize accessibility. DCs are encouraged and supported to present at international conferences and participate in international research networks.

Intersectoral

Secondments and co-supervision connect universities with university hospitals, digital health SMEs, and other non-academic partners. DCs gain first-hand experience of clinical workflows, regulatory compliance processes and product-development lifecycles, which fosters a shared language between themselves, clinicians and regulators.

Interdisciplinary

Each DC is exposed to computer science, statistics, medicine, law/regulation and human-centred design/social sciences through joint courses, co-supervision and cross- work-package collaborations, reflecting the sociotechnical nature of trustworthy causal AI in healthcare.

1.3.4 Special training elements of the network

Local training at host organizations

Each host institution provides structured doctoral training through its graduate or doctoral school. This training includes core scientific courses and seminars, as well as modules on transferable skills such as research ethics, gender and diversity, and open science. Wherever possible, these courses are made available on-site or online to DCs from other beneficiary institutions, thereby increasing efficiency and coherence. Individual research projects, group meetings, journal clubs, and local clinical seminars ensure that DCs are fully integrated into vibrant research and clinical environments.

1.4.2 Quality of supervision for DN

Supervision in the DN is organised around a multi-layered structure that combines day- to-day guidance at the host institution with network-wide monitoring and support:

• Each DC has a main academic supervisor at the recruiting beneficiary and at least one co-supervisor or mentor from another sector (hospital, SME or other non-academic partner). Where appropriate, an additional mentor from a complementary discipline (e.g. law/regulation, human-centred design) is included. Together, they form an Individual Training Panel (ITP) or supervisory committee.

• Within the first three months, the ITP and DC jointly agree a Personal Career Development Plan (PCDP), specifying research objectives, training needs, secondments, open-science commitments and career goals. The PCDP is reviewed at least every six months and updated when needed; key milestones are aligned with host doctoral-school requirements and network deliverables, and PCDP updates are validated through the Supervisory Board as part of training monitoring activities.

Day-to-day supervision follows a clear and consistent policy across the consortium:

• Regular meetings between DCs and their main supervisors (typically every 2–4 weeks) focus on scientific progress, skills development and well-being.

• ITP meetings (in person or online) are held at least twice per year, often aligned with network-wide events, to review PCDPs, training progress, secondment planning and career perspectives.

• Supervisors operate an open-door communication culture, encouraging DCs to raise scientific or personal concerns early. Short ad hoc meetings and online interactions complement formal supervision sessions and provide a two-way feedback channel.

Progress and review procedures are embedded in project governance:

• The Supervisory Board (SB) oversees the overall supervision strategy and ensures that PCDPs, secondments and training objectives are implemented consistently across sites, in line with the MSCA Guidelines on Supervision.

• Training and supervision quality are monitored through annual progress reports, PCDP updates and anonymous feedback questionnaires completed by DCs after major training events.

• Clear procedures for conflict prevention and resolution are included in the Consortium Agreement (e.g. two-step escalation from local resolution within the ITP to intervention by the SB and, if needed, an external ombudsperson), ensuring that problems can be addressed in a timely and confidential manner.

Supervision explicitly includes career development, integration and well-being. DCs are supported in building professional networks (e.g. conference participation, joint publications, involvement in standards or guideline activities) and are encouraged to co- supervise MSc students or contribute to teaching, under guidance. Integration into local research and clinical groups is fostered through lab meetings, journal clubs and clinical seminars, ensuring that each DC works within a vibrant environment rather than in isolation.

Although the project is a standard Doctoral Network (not an Industrial Doctorate or Joint Doctorate scheme), each DC benefits from this structured co-supervision team, which provides complementary intersectoral and interdisciplinary guidance comparable in quality to mandatory joint-supervision schemes in industrial and joint doctorates.
